title: How your eyes turn light into sight
description: Your eye is a camera that focuses light onto a living sensor — and the picture it forms there is upside down.

body.heading: A camera made of living tissue
paragraphs: The eye works like a camera. Light enters through the clear cornea at the front, which does most of the bending of the rays, then passes through the pupil — the hole whose size the coloured iris adjusts, widening in dim light and narrowing in bright light.
Behind the pupil sits the lens. It fine-tunes the focus: tiny muscles pull it flatter for distant objects and let it round up for near ones, so the image lands sharply on the back of the eye.

body.heading: The retina catches the picture
paragraphs: The image is projected onto the retina, a thin layer of light-sensitive cells — and it arrives upside down. The retina holds two kinds of sensors: rods, which work in dim light but see no colour, and cones, which need brighter light and come in three types for colour vision.

Each sensor converts light into electrical signals that travel down the optic nerve to the brain. Where the nerve leaves the eye there are no sensors at all, leaving a blind spot your brain silently fills in.

body.heading: The brain builds the view
paragraphs: Seeing is done by the brain, not the eye. It flips the upside-down image the right way up, merges the slightly different pictures from two eyes into one with depth, and corrects for colour under different lighting.

That construction work explains optical illusions: they are cases where the brain's shortcuts — assuming light comes from above, or that lines continue — are fooled by a drawing designed to trip them. It also explains why you never notice your blind spot, and why two eyes beat one: each covers the other's gaps, while their overlap measures the world in depth.

takeaway: The cornea and lens focus light onto the retina, where rods and cones turn it into nerve signals; the brain assembles those signals into sight.
